metaTitle: Spruce: see what you can safely delete on your Mac or PC
metaDescription: Spruce checks your disk in the background and shows how much space you can safely free, what each cleanup does and if you can undo it. For macOS and Windows.
metaImageAlt: Spruce's icon and headline beside its overview, which shows the space it can free and its recommendations
ogTagline: Open it and see how much space you can safely free.
heroTitle:
Know what you can delete,
before you delete it.
heroLead: Spruce checks your disk in the background. Open it and it already knows how much space you can safely free, which items it would remove, why, and what happens afterwards.
heroMeta: macOS (Apple silicon, Intel) · Windows (x64, arm64) · v{version} · Free and open source · Interface in Simplified Chinese
shotOverviewAlt: The overview: 27.5 GB that can be freed, the startup disk, and recommendation cards such as the Xcode build cache and installers in Downloads
stepCheckBody: When the window opens and every few hours, only on power and when the computer isn't busy. The checks only read; they never delete anything.
stepExplainBody: Each card is one action: what it is, why it's safe, what happens afterwards, and whether it can be undone.
stepActBody: On macOS, moves to the Trash happen at once with an Undo. Anything that can't be undone asks first.
recBody: Instead of hundreds of categories to tick, Spruce shows a few cards sorted by size and safety, such as "Xcode build cache, not built for 40 days" or "2 installers in Downloads whose apps are installed". Items that need your judgement, like caches of running apps or projects with uncommitted changes, are kept apart.
shotToastAlt: Recommendation cards for the Xcode build cache, app caches and installers in Downloads, with the message "Moved 2.1 GB to the Trash · Undo" at the bottom
undoTitle: Changed your mind? Put it back
undoBody: On macOS, a move to the Trash shows "Moved 2.1 GB to the Trash · Undo". History can put back any move of the last 30 days that's still in the Trash, and never overwrites what's there now.
shotHistoryAlt: History: today's and yesterday's records, each move still in the Trash with a Put back button, and filters by kind of clean
spaceBody: A map of any folder, sized by what each item takes, and a list of the largest files. Open a folder, reveal it in Finder or Explorer, or move it to the Trash.
shotSpaceAlt: Space Lens: a map of the 255.5 GB home folder, with Library, Projects and Movies as the largest blocks, beside a list of its folders by size
growthBody: Once a day Spruce notes the size of the main locations, such as caches, Downloads and project folders, and keeps 90 days. It shows what grew over 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days, for example "~/Library/Caches/com.apple.Safari grew 6.2 GB since Wednesday".
shotGrowthAlt: Recent changes over 7 days: the Safari cache up 6.2 GB, the Xcode build cache up 4.3 GB and Downloads up 2.8 GB since Wednesday
uninstallTitle: Remove an app and what it left behind
uninstallBody: Pick an app to see its support files, caches, preferences and saved state, then choose which go with it. On macOS everything goes to the Trash and can be put back. On Windows, Spruce runs the program's own uninstaller first, then offers what it left in your user folder.
shotUninstallAlt: Uninstall: Blender picked from the list of apps, with its application support files, cache, preferences and saved window state ticked, 1.3 GB to move to the Trash
autoTitle: Rules that only use the Trash
autoBody: Four rules, all off until you turn them on: old app caches, installers whose apps are installed, build output of idle projects, and unfinished downloads. They never run a command and never delete for good. Every run is recorded in History and can be put back.
autoPoint2: Never takes back an item you restored
shotAutoAlt: Automatic cleaning settings: the four rules, two of them on, and the weekly summary
menubarBody: The menu bar shows free space and changes its icon when space runs low. An optional notification tells you when the startup disk drops below a level you set.
trayAlertAlt: Spruce's menu bar icon when space runs low
devTitle: Build output and tool caches, without touching your work
devBody: Spruce lists each project with its last activity, the size of its `node_modules`, `target`, `.next` and other build output, and its Git state. A project with uncommitted changes is never selected or cleaned, and Git is asked again right before anything is deleted.
devPoint1: Xcode, Homebrew, npm, pnpm, Go, Cargo, Gradle, JetBrains and more: with the tool's own clean command where it has one
devPoint2: Node, Rust, Maven, Gradle, CocoaPods, SwiftPM, Python, .NET, Zig and Flutter projects
devPoint3: When Git is missing or fails, the project is marked "unknown" and left unselected
shotDevAlt: Projects with their build output, last activity, size and Git state; blog, which has uncommitted changes, is not selected
cliTitle: The same checks from a terminal
cliBody: The app is also a command line: `scan`, `recommendations`, `clean`, `projects`, `history` and `restore`, all with `--json`. It only deletes with `--yes`.
cliCommentScan: What can be freed, as JSON
cliCommentProjects: Projects, their build output and Git state
cliReadme: Every command, and how to put `spruce` on your PATH
shotHealthAlt: Health: live cards for CPU, memory, disk, network, battery and the system, under the setting of the high CPU alert
detailJunkBody: App and browser caches, logs, crash reports, temporary files and unfinished downloads. Browser cookies, history and logins are not touched.
detailMaintBody: Flush the DNS cache, check the Spotlight index, refresh Quick Look, rebuild icon caches, repair "Open With", optimize app databases. On Windows: DNS, icons, thumbnails, stale "Open With" entries, Windows Search.
detailHealthBody: CPU, memory, disk, network and battery in real time, the processes using the most, and a banner when one process uses too much CPU for too long. Spruce only shows processes; it never ends them.
detailHistoryBody: Every clean, uninstall, maintenance run and automatic clean, with what it freed and what it couldn't.
detailExclBody: Add folders or patterns Spruce must never touch.
detailLowBody: Off by default. When on, Spruce tells you once when the startup disk drops below your level, and at most once a day.
safetyTitle: It tells you before it does anything you can't undo
safety1Body: Background checks never delete, never run commands and never ask for a permission.
safety2Body: Each card says whether it moves to the Trash (can be undone), deletes something that is regenerated, or runs a tool's command. The last two always ask first.
safety3Title: Checked again at the last moment
safety3Body: Every item is checked again right before it is moved or deleted. One that changed since the check, is in use, or belongs to a project with new changes is skipped.
safety4Body: Spruce only removes items inside the folders it checked and honors your exclusions. It never follows a link elsewhere. It never deletes for good inside the system, keychains, iCloud Drive, Mail, `~/.ssh`, Documents, Desktop or Pictures: there it can only use the Trash.
safety5Body: Spruce never runs commands, deletes for good, empties the Trash, uninstalls or runs maintenance by itself. Automatic rules, if you turn them on, only move files to the Trash.
privacyBody: No account. What Spruce learns about your disk (settings, history, size snapshots) stays in its data folder, readable only by you.
dlBody: Free and open source under the MIT license. Each release has the disk images, the installers, the install scripts and their SHA-256 checksums on GitHub.
dlLang: Spruce's interface is in Simplified Chinese.
dlMacBody: Download the disk image for your Mac, open it and drag Spruce to Applications. It is signed and notarized by Apple.
dlWinBody: Download the x64 installer for most PCs, or the arm64 one for a Windows on Arm PC, and run it. It installs for your user only.
dlWinUnsigned: The Windows installers aren't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may warn you. Choose "More info", then "Run anyway".
dlWinLimits: On Windows there is no tray icon, no undo and no automatic rules yet.
faqAskFirstQ: Will Spruce delete anything without asking?
faqAskFirstA: No. Checks only read. Moving to the Trash on macOS happens at once and can be undone. Deleting for good, running a tool's command and emptying the Trash always ask first. Automatic rules are off until you turn them on, and only move to the Trash.
faqRestoreA: On macOS, press Undo, or use Put Back in History for moves of the last 30 days that are still in the Trash. Items deleted for good, mostly caches and build output that are regenerated, can't be restored; their cards say so. On Windows, restore from the Recycle Bin.
faqBackgroundA: A read-only check at most every 6 hours, only on power, not in Low Power Mode, and not when the computer is hot or busy. You can turn it off in Settings › General.
faqDataQ: Does Spruce send my data anywhere?
faqDataA: No account is needed, and everything Spruce records stays in its data folder on your computer.
faqDiskAccessQ: Why does it ask for Full Disk Access?
faqDiskAccessA: It's optional. macOS needs it for Spruce to optimize the Safari and Mail databases, read the Trash, find some apps' leftovers and include other apps' containers. Spruce never asks for it from a background check.
faqPasswordQ: Why does maintenance ask for my password?
faqPasswordA: Flushing the DNS cache, and rebuilding a broken Spotlight index, need administrator rights. macOS asks once per run. The other tasks don't.
faqCodeA: Only build output such as `node_modules` or `target`, and never in a project with uncommitted changes. Git is checked again right before deleting.
faqWindowsA: No tray icon (closing the window quits). Background checks run only while it's open. Moves to the Recycle Bin are confirmed and have no Undo. No automatic rules. Everything else is the same.
faqEnglishQ: Is the interface available in English?
faqEnglishA: Not yet: the interface is in Simplified Chinese.
faqLinuxA: No. Spruce is for macOS and Windows.
faqUpdateA: Download the new version from this page or GitHub Releases, or run the install command again. Spruce doesn't update itself.
faqPriceA: No. Spruce is free and open source under the MIT license.
